title: Rep Range Compass
user: A strength trainee using double progression who needs to know the next set's target and whether a weight increase is earned, without moving their health history to a hosted service.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In the self-hosted workout-tracker discussion, users call out missing Apple Health import, unclear current-set position, and incomplete mobile workflow.
A user explains that common 3×8–12 double progression cannot be represented because a weight increase fires after the bottom of the range rather than all sets reaching the top.

recurrence: Two independent fitness-tracker communities identify the same high-frequency moment: recording a set while deciding whether to progress. It occurs every workout for lifters using rep ranges.
current_workaround: Use a full workout tracker plus a notes field, spreadsheet, or mental arithmetic to remember rep-range state.
incumbents_and_gap: wger, Hevy, Strong, and Ryot record workouts, but their broad programs obscure the narrow next-set/next-weight decision and can require an account or server.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA with one exercise card: log weight/reps/RIR, apply a configurable rep-range rule, show the next-set cue and export/import CSV. Non-goals: exercise library, social feed, coaching, nutrition, or medical metrics.
success_measure: In a four-week pilot, 70% of users log at least eight sessions and can answer 'increase or repeat?' without a separate note in 90% of logged exercises.
monetization: one-time — a focused personal log should keep data local and not make training history contingent on a subscription.
constraints: All data stays in IndexedDB by default; CSV import must be local; clearly state that progression suggestions are configurable arithmetic, not coaching or medical advice.
why_distinct: It is a progression decision card, not another full workout catalogue or AI fitness coach.

title: Meal List Boundaries
user: A household planning meals for more than one home or pickup context who needs a weekly menu to produce the right shopping list without leaking one household's items into another.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The author of a local-first family meal planner receives a direct reply that this is an active pain for the commenter.
A Tandoor user has two homes and two lists but cannot scope each Home Assistant connector to only its own household's list.

recurrence: The need appears in both a local-first meal-planning launch and a detailed multi-home request; meal plans repeatedly cross household, store, and pickup boundaries.
current_workaround: Duplicate recipes/lists, manually deselect items, or maintain separate chats and shopping apps per household.
incumbents_and_gap: Mealie, Tandoor, Paprika, and AnyList cover recipes and lists, but list ownership/boundaries are usually a sync setting rather than a visible planning primitive.
smallest_useful_product: A local-first weekly board that assigns each meal and ingredient to a named household/list, generates separate printable or shareable lists, and records a simple 'bought' state. Non-goals: recipe scraping, delivery ordering, price comparison, and cloud accounts.
success_measure: At least 80% of pilot weeks produce two or more correctly separated lists with no manually copied ingredient between them.
monetization: one-time — families need a durable household utility, not a recurring charge for a grocery checklist.
constraints: Local export/import and QR handoff must work without a central account; avoid retailer integrations and retain no dietary or location data.
why_distinct: The primary object is a boundary-aware handoff from plan to the right buyer, not a generic recipe manager.

title: Scaled Cook Card
user: A home cook scaling a familiar recipe who needs every preparation step to retain the correctly scaled ingredient quantities while cooking hands-free.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A 2026 self-hosted recipe-manager launch specifically emphasizes cook mode and a cook journal, showing that using recipes during cooking remains distinct from simply storing them.
A Cookbook user asks to bind ingredients into preparation steps so scaled amounts appear directly where the cook needs them.

recurrence: Separate recipe products are adding cook mode while users still ask for ingredient-to-step binding; the failure happens repeatedly whenever recipe yield changes.
current_workaround: Do arithmetic while cooking, annotate screenshots, or repeatedly scroll between an ingredient list and steps.
incumbents_and_gap: Paprika, Mealie, Tandoor, Cooklang, and Cookbook store recipes; many offer scaling, but a compact local execution card with step-level bound values and post-cook corrections is not their core artifact.
smallest_useful_product: Static/offline web app that imports a small YAML/JSON recipe, scales servings, renders bound ingredient tokens in each step, and saves actual yield/substitutions locally. Non-goals: web recipe scraping, meal planning, nutrition claims, or social recipe publishing.
success_measure: In a pilot of 20 cooked recipes, users report zero manual quantity recalculations and save corrections on at least 30% of recipes.
monetization: one-time — portable recipe files and offline kitchen use are more credible without a content subscription.
constraints: Use user-authored/imported recipes only; no copyrighted site extraction; large touch controls and screen-wake behavior must degrade safely when unsupported.
why_distinct: It treats a recipe as a live, scaled procedure rather than a collection to browse.

title: Finish One Pantry
user: A household that buys repeat packages (milk, rice, detergent) and wants a low-effort way to know when a replacement belongs on the list.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A commenter doubts people can keep a pantry app synchronized with reality for more than a week, directly identifying maintenance burden as the obstacle.
A Grocy user describes the two-step friction of finishing a package and opening a replacement, and asks for that single event to update stock correctly.

recurrence: The same inventory-sync failure is voiced in a public launch discussion and an established pantry project's feature request; it affects every consumable package.
current_workaround: Maintain a detailed inventory briefly, write a separate shopping note when something runs out, or discover the shortage during meal preparation.
incumbents_and_gap: Grocy, Pantry Check, and iPantry model detailed stock and expiry. Their accuracy depends on data entry; they do not center the one real-world 'finished/opened replacement' gesture.
smallest_useful_product: Offline mobile PWA with a pinned shelf of recurring packages and one Finish button that decrements a simple reserve count and adds an item to a local list at the chosen threshold. Non-goals: barcode database, receipt OCR, expiry tracking, recipes, or household accounting.
success_measure: After 30 days, 60% of pilot users still record at least three finish events per week and report fewer than one surprise stockout for tracked items.
monetization: free — the tiny, local interaction is best validated through adoption; optional one-time household sharing could follow.
constraints: No product database or retailer data is needed; exportable local JSON; design must work one-handed and tolerate missed events without falsely claiming inventory precision.
why_distinct: It deliberately rejects exhaustive pantry inventory in favor of a single sustainable replenishment signal.

title: Bed Season Ledger
user: A small-space or backyard gardener who needs to remember what was actually planted in each bed and turn local frost dates into a short, editable next-actions list.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A 2026 garden-planner launch is explicitly framed around climate-aware scheduling, indicating demand for schedule help rather than plant encyclopedias.
The long-running request for a garden/plant tracker asks for templates, planting and harvesting dates, spacing, inventory effects, and scheduled care—scope that remains outside pantry tools.

recurrence: Garden planning continues to appear as a dedicated product category while a household-planning project's request shows the persistent need to join actual planting, timing, and harvest records.
current_workaround: Paper bed sketches, seed packets, generic planting calendars, and spreadsheets that lose the record of what really happened.
incumbents_and_gap: GrowVeg, Seedtime, Gardenate, and various plant trackers provide planning or reference data; a minimal local season ledger linking bed history to editable climate windows remains unnecessarily heavyweight.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA for up to 20 beds: place a crop/variety and date, enter last/first-frost dates, generate a tiny upcoming-actions list, and export a season PDF. Non-goals: plant diagnosis, marketplace data, camera identification, and automatic weather claims.
success_measure: By season end, 70% of pilot gardeners can answer what occupied each bed and complete at least five scheduled actions from the app.
monetization: one-time — a seasonal personal record has durable value but does not need hosted data collection.
constraints: Show all scheduling as editable heuristics; bundle only openly licensed crop timing defaults; no claims of local weather or pest expertise.
why_distinct: It is a lightweight record of the actual garden plus next actions, not a plant-ID app or a generic calendar.

title: Home Care Evidence
user: A homeowner turning an inspection finding or completed repair into a repeatable maintenance record that another household member can understand years later.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A 2026 home-maintenance tracker launch is explicitly positioned around preventing costly repairs, showing continued demand for maintenance follow-through.
A Homebox user reports that duplicating a maintenance entry from the global view fails, illustrating the fragility of recurring-maintenance workflows in a mature home-inventory product.

recurrence: New home-maintenance products and active maintenance workflow reports both point to recurring, high-cost household work that must survive time and handoff.
current_workaround: Keep an inspection PDF, scattered photos, invoices, calendar reminders, and a vague to-do item in different locations.
incumbents_and_gap: Homebox, Centriq, Dwellable, and spreadsheets inventory assets or schedule tasks; they do not make the compact why/done-proof/next-due maintenance packet the central local artifact.
smallest_useful_product: Local PWA with a maintenance card containing the observed issue, photos, vendor/DIY note, receipt attachment, due interval, and printable one-page history. Non-goals: contractor marketplace, inspection diagnosis, smart-home integrations, or cloud storage.
success_measure: In six months, pilot households can retrieve proof and the next due date for 90% of tracked home-care items in under one minute.
monetization: one-time — records should remain available when a homeowner is not actively buying repairs.
constraints: Attachments stay on device unless explicitly exported; encrypt exported archive option; no safety, building-code, or professional repair advice.
why_distinct: It preserves maintenance evidence and context, rather than being another task list or home-service lead generator.

title: Claim-Ready Homebook
user: A renter or homeowner who wants an insurance-ready, portable record of belongings, serials, receipts, and storage locations before a stressful loss.

evidence.quote_or_summary: In a ClaimVault discussion, a user says insurance claims and all the associated files are painful but rejects paying an ongoing $20/month outside an active claim.
A Homebox user needs a main product and its spare parts linked while stored in different places, a concrete example of how location and ownership records diverge.

recurrence: Claims are infrequent but severe; two separate home-record discussions expose the need for durable proof without a permanent subscription.
current_workaround: Phone photos, folders of receipts, a generic inventory app, and a rushed reconstruction after a loss.
incumbents_and_gap: Homebox, Sortly, Encircle, and insurer portals manage inventory, but recurring cloud billing and insurer lock-in make a self-contained, portable claim packet less available.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA for item photos, value/date/serial/receipt, container and room location, plus an encrypted export that creates a readable PDF/CSV claim packet. Non-goals: submitting claims, valuation guarantees, cloud backup, or insurance advice.
success_measure: A pilot user can create an export for 50 items in under ten minutes and open it on a second device without an account.
monetization: one-time — the strongest value proposition is permanent access to the user's own evidence.
constraints: Local-only by default; optional encrypted export with user-held passphrase; communicate that insurer requirements and valuations vary.
why_distinct: It produces an owner-controlled claim packet, not a hosted inventory catalogue or claims intermediary.

title: Chore Rulebook
user: A household sharing recurring chores who needs transparent assignment rules and a lightweight completion history, without gamifying domestic work or requiring every member to create an account.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A 2025 launch presents Roomsy specifically as a better way to manage household chores, confirming an active market for shared domestic coordination.
A Grocy request asks for durations on chores and meal-plan items, showing that simple recurring-task checks omit the effort and planning information households need.

recurrence: A current dedicated chore product and a feature request inside household-management software both show coordination needs beyond a flat todo list.
current_workaround: Whiteboards, rotating verbal agreements, shared reminders, or a generic family task app whose assignments gradually become opaque.
incumbents_and_gap: Tody, Sweepy, OurHome, Cozi, and Grocy provide checklists, streaks, or points. They rarely expose a simple, inspectable rule for rotation, availability, estimated effort, and missed-turn recovery.
smallest_useful_product: Offline shared-device PWA with named people, chores, interval/effort, rotation or fixed-owner rule, a 'why assigned' explanation, and a local history export. Non-goals: points, rewards, surveillance, chat, or account-based family social features.
success_measure: After 30 days, 75% of completed chores are recorded and each participant can correctly explain their next assignment without asking another person.
monetization: one-time — it is a household appliance-like utility and should not make coordination dependent on a subscription.
constraints: No child profiling or behavioral scoring; device-local data and printable QR pairing; support accessibility and plain-language assignments.
why_distinct: Its value is explainable allocation rules and effort balance, not a prettier chore checklist or reward system.

title: LAN Family Dayboard
user: A household that wants a shared tablet or e-ink display for today's events and responsibilities without creating cloud accounts for every family member.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A 2026 Show HN explicitly offers an open-source, no-account calendar intended for an entire household.
An earlier Show HN for a shared family calendar demonstrates the same dedicated household-calendar demand in a separate project.

recurrence: Two independent household-calendar launches, two years apart, are explicitly framed as shared family coordination rather than personal scheduling.
current_workaround: Share Google/Apple calendars, keep a paper calendar, or use a family-organizer subscription and deal with account invitations.
incumbents_and_gap: Google Calendar, Apple Family Sharing, Cozi, Skylight, and DAKboard offer calendars or displays, but a tiny local-LAN day display with no sign-in and a portable ICS input is uncommon.
smallest_useful_product: Static web dayboard that reads manually imported ICS files or a user-run LAN feed, renders a big today/tomorrow view and chores, and prints a weekly sheet. Non-goals: hosted calendar sync, messaging, contacts, or a proprietary display device.
success_measure: In a two-week household trial, participants consult the display on at least ten days and report fewer than two missed shared events attributable to calendar visibility.
monetization: free — compatibility and local deployment are the initial adoption goal; a paid preconfigured display image could follow.
constraints: Parse ICS locally and safely; never scrape third-party calendars or store credentials; provide a clear manual-refresh path for offline displays.
why_distinct: It is a no-account ambient display, not a replacement cloud calendar or a family social network.

title: Bill Runway
user: A person or caregiver who needs to see upcoming invoices, due dates, and cash needed before income arrives, without connecting bank accounts or adopting a full budgeting system.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The author describes building a budget tool because their partner kept complaining about spreadsheets, a direct signal that spreadsheet cashflow planning remains burdensome.
A user managing bills for themself and their mother needs a clear overview of invoices due, then to pay them after income arrives.

recurrence: The cashflow-before-payday problem appears in both a personal spreadsheet-replacement story and an explicit caregiver invoice-management request.
current_workaround: Spreadsheets, calendar reminders, paper bills, and a full expense app that starts after a transaction is already paid.
incumbents_and_gap: YNAB, Actual Budget, Firefly III, and Monarch handle broad budgeting. Their depth is unnecessary for the narrow question: which dated obligations are covered by the money I expect before each due date?
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA for a list of bills/invoices, expected income dates, one-time or recurring due rules, and a timeline that flags an uncovered amount; export a one-page payment run. Non-goals: bank aggregation, payments, credit scoring, debt advice, or tax calculation.
success_measure: In a 60-day pilot, 80% of entered bills are marked paid by their due date and users can identify any uncovered due-date window in under one minute.
monetization: one-time — people avoiding subscription creep and bank sharing need a durable local planner.
constraints: No financial-institution credentials; use decimal-safe currency arithmetic; label forecasts as user-entered planning data, not financial advice.
why_distinct: It is a due-date cash runway, not a general ledger, expense tracker, or banking dashboard.

title: Manual Spend Replay
user: A privacy-minded person who intentionally enters purchases manually and needs fast repeat-entry plus a plain replay of what changed since their last review.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A commenter using a local expense tracker values manual entry because it builds spending habits and notes that repeat categories benefit from predictive form filling.
Actual Budget's high-discussion formula-card/rules feedback shows users extending a budgeting app with spreadsheet-like custom views to answer personal questions.

recurrence: Manual-entry advocates need low-friction repetition while sophisticated budget users keep recreating bespoke review views; both indicate a gap between input and reflection.
current_workaround: Use spreadsheets, a full budget app, bank sync, or manually filter transaction lists to reconstruct the last few days.
incumbents_and_gap: Actual Budget, Firefly III, YNAB, and expense apps emphasize accounts, envelopes, reports, or bank integration. They do not prioritize offline repeat-entry followed by a small chronological 'what changed?' replay.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA with quick amount/payee/category entry, local suggestions based on prior entries, and a review screen that narrates changes since the last check-in by category and merchant. Non-goals: bank connections, receipt OCR, investment tracking, tax reports, or AI categorization.
success_measure: After four weeks, 65% of pilot users enter purchases on at least 20 days and complete a weekly replay without exporting to a spreadsheet.
monetization: one-time — manual, local budgeting should not add another recurring financial commitment.
constraints: All transactions remain on device; use export/import with no analytics; currency/rounding must be deterministic; never frame insights as financial advice.
why_distinct: It optimizes deliberate entry and review cadence rather than duplicating bank-connected budgeting products.

title: Dose Chain Log
user: A person taking several medicines at common times or with an after-taken interval who needs to confirm a group quickly and schedule follow-ups from the actual taken time.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A 2026 launch for an open-source Android medication reminder shows continuing demand for a privacy-respecting alternative in this sensitive category.
A MedTimer user taking around ten medicines says individual confirmation is annoying and requests grouped taken/skipped/reschedule actions.

recurrence: Medication-reminder tools continue to launch, while users with multiple medicines identify batch confirmation as a repeated, accessibility-relevant friction point.
current_workaround: Tap many individual reminders, set separate phone alarms, or use a general medication app that treats every dose as an independent event.
incumbents_and_gap: Medisafe, MyTherapy, Apple Health Medications, and MedTimer provide reminders. A constrained local event log centered on group confirmation and actual-time follow-up chains is a smaller unmet workflow.
smallest_useful_product: Android app with user-configured medicine labels, grouped time windows, taken/skipped/late event logging, and optional follow-up timers anchored to a recorded taken time. Non-goals: dosage recommendations, interaction checking, prescription management, caregiver surveillance, or medical records integration.
success_measure: In a 30-day opt-in pilot, users with three or more concurrent medicines record 85% of configured group events and need fewer than two taps per group confirmation on median.
monetization: one-time — sensitive adherence data should not require ongoing cloud billing or advertising.
constraints: Sensitive health data remains on device and is exportable only by the user; notification reliability must follow Android requirements; include clear non-medical-advice and emergency guidance boundaries.
why_distinct: It handles the temporal relationship among already prescribed doses, not diagnosis, prescription, or generic reminder gamification.
